title: Tautavel Man, one of the oldest inhabitants of France
text:
A very, very long time ago, long before kings, castles and even the Gauls, humans already lived in the land that is now France.

In 1971, in a cave in the Pyrenees, near the village of Tautavel, archaeologists made an amazing discovery: the skull of a human who lived about 450,000 years ago! They called him "Tautavel Man". He is one of the oldest known inhabitants of France.

Tautavel Man was not quite like us. He belonged to an older human species, close to [Homo erectus]. He was smaller than us, about 1.65 metres tall, with a sloping forehead and big bony eyebrows. But he walked upright and already made tools!

The cave where he was found, the Caune de l'Arago, overlooked a valley. It was a perfect lookout for spotting herds of animals. At that time, the region was full of horses, reindeer, bison, wild sheep, rhinoceroses and even elephants!

These humans were [hunter-gatherers]. They hunted, and collected plants, fruits and roots. They made stone tools by striking pebbles to make them sharp, like [hand axes], big almond-shaped stones used to cut meat, scrape skins or break bones.

In the cave, archaeologists found thousands of animal bones. But they found no traces of fire in the oldest layers: these humans probably did not yet know how to control it. Fire appeared a bit later, about 400,000 years ago, and it changed everything: people could keep warm, cook meat and protect themselves from wild animals.

Today, digging continues every summer at Tautavel, and a large museum lets visitors discover the life of these distant ancestors. You can see a reconstruction of Tautavel Man, who seems to look at you across the ages.

Later, other humans arrived: the [Neanderthals], and then, about 45,000 years ago, our own species, [Homo sapiens]. They are the ones who would paint the caves...

title: The paintings of the Lascaux cave
text:
On the 12th of September 1940, four teenagers were walking in a forest near Montignac, in the Dordogne. Their dog, Robot, disappeared down a hole! Trying to get him back, the boys widened the hole and slipped underground with a small lamp. What they saw left them speechless: walls covered with gigantic painted animals, in red, black and yellow!

They had discovered the Lascaux cave, one of the greatest treasures of prehistory. It is sometimes called "the Sistine Chapel of prehistory".

These paintings were made about 17,000 years ago by [Homo sapiens], humans like us. At that time, it was the end of the last [Ice Age]: it was much colder than today.

There are almost 2,000 figures: horses, deer, bison, ibex, and huge aurochs, wild cattle that no longer exist. The biggest bull is more than 5 metres long! There are also mysterious signs: dots, lines and squares.

How did these artists do it? They used natural [pigments]: ochre for red and yellow, charcoal and manganese for black. They applied them with their fingers, with pads of moss, or by blowing them through a hollow tube, like a spray gun! To light the darkness, they used lamps burning animal fat. To paint the ceilings, they even built wooden scaffolding.

Why did they paint these animals? We don't really know. Maybe for ceremonies, to bring luck in hunting, or to tell stories. What is certain is that these artists were incredibly talented: the animals seem to move in the flickering light of the flames.

The cave was opened to the public in 1948. But the breath and warmth of thousands of visitors damaged the paintings: mould appeared. In 1963, the cave was closed forever to protect it. Today, visitors can see perfect copies, like Lascaux IV, and admire these masterpieces without harming them.

The Lascaux cave is a [UNESCO World Heritage] site. In 1994, an even older cave was discovered in the Ardèche, the Chauvet cave, with paintings 36,000 years old!

title: The standing stones of Carnac
text:
In Brittany, near the town of Carnac, there is something incredible: thousands of big standing stones, lined up in long rows over several kilometres, like an army of giants frozen in place! There are more than 3,000 of them. These are the Carnac stones.

These stones were raised about 6,000 years ago, during the [Neolithic]. It was a very important period: humans had learned to farm the land and raise animals. They no longer had to move all the time to hunt. They lived in villages, grew wheat and barley, kept sheep, goats, cows and pigs, and made pottery.

These big stones are called [megaliths], which means "big stones" in Greek. A single standing stone is called a menhir, a Breton word meaning "long stone". There are also dolmens, "stone tables": big slabs laid on top of standing stones, which were used as tombs.

How did they move stones that sometimes weighed several tonnes, without machines or wheels? Probably with lots of people, ropes, wooden logs to roll them on, and levers. It needed incredible organisation! The biggest menhir in France, the "Great Broken Menhir" of Locmariaquer, was over 20 metres high and weighed about 280 tonnes, as much as 50 elephants!

What were the alignments for? It's a great mystery. Places for ceremonies? A calendar to follow the sun and the seasons? Monuments to honour ancestors? Scientists are still making guesses.

There are lots of legends. One says that the stones of Carnac are Roman soldiers turned to stone by a saint! But careful: the megaliths are much older than the Romans... and even than the Gauls!

Another common mistake: in the comic books, Obelix delivers menhirs. In reality, the Gauls lived 3,000 years after the menhirs were built!

Today, the Carnac stones attract visitors from all over the world, fascinated by these silent stones that keep their secret.

title: The Gauls and the founding of Marseille
text:
About 2,600 years ago, the land of France was home to many peoples that the Romans would later call the [Gauls]. They were part of a large group of peoples, the [Celts], who lived across much of Europe.

The Gauls were not one single country. They were about sixty different peoples, each with its own territory and chiefs: the Arverni in the Auvergne, the Parisii around Paris (who gave their name to the city!), the Aedui in Burgundy... They sometimes fought each other.

Contrary to what people often think, the Gauls were not savages living in the forest! They were excellent craftsmen and farmers. They invented the wooden barrel to store wine and beer. They made superb gold jewellery, like torcs, rigid necklaces. They were very good blacksmiths and made iron ploughs. They even struck their own coins.

Their priests were called [druids]. They were also judges, teachers and scholars. They knew about the stars and plants, and picked mistletoe from oak trees with a golden sickle. But they did not write down their knowledge: everything was learned by heart!

Around 600 BC, Greek sailors from the city of Phocaea (in today's Turkey) arrived on the Mediterranean coast. A legend says that their leader, Protis, arrived on the very day when Gyptis, the daughter of a Gaulish king, was to choose her husband. She handed a cup to Protis, the stranger, to show she had chosen him! The king gave them land by the sea, where they founded a city: Massalia, which would become... Marseille! It is the oldest city in France.

The Greeks brought vines and olive trees to Gaul, as well as writing, and trade with the whole Mediterranean world. Marseille became a great trading port.

The Gauls left many traces in the French language: words like "chêne" (oak), "mouton" (sheep), "charrue" (plough) and "ruche" (beehive) come from Gaulish!

title: Vercingetorix and the Battle of Alesia
text:
In 58 BC, a very ambitious Roman general, [Julius Caesar], began the conquest of Gaul. He wanted to become rich, famous and powerful in Rome. With his well-trained legions, he gradually conquered the Gaulish peoples, who were often divided.

In 52 BC, a young chief of the Arverni people named Vercingetorix did something extraordinary: he united almost all the Gaulish peoples against Rome. He was only about twenty years old! His name probably meant something like "great king of warriors".

Vercingetorix used a clever tactic called "scorched earth": he had villages and crops burned so that the Roman army would find nothing to eat. At Gergovia, near today's Clermont-Ferrand, he even defeated Caesar!

But the same year, Vercingetorix and about 80,000 warriors took refuge in Alesia, a fortified town on a hill in Burgundy. Caesar decided to surround them. In just a few weeks, his soldiers built an incredible line of fortifications more than 15 kilometres long all around the hill, with ditches, traps and towers. Then they built a second line facing outwards, to protect themselves from a Gaulish relief army!

Inside Alesia, food ran out. A huge Gaulish relief army arrived, but despite several attacks, it could not break through the Roman lines.

Defeated, Vercingetorix surrendered to save his men. Tradition says he rode up in his armour, threw his weapons at Caesar's feet and sat down in silence. He was taken to Rome as a prisoner, where he stayed locked up for six years before being paraded in Caesar's triumph and then executed.

After Alesia, Gaul became Roman. In the 19th century, Vercingetorix became a national hero, a symbol of courage and resistance. A huge statue of him stands on the site of Alesia today, along with a big museum about the battle.

And Asterix? It's a funny comic book, but made up: there was never a little Gaulish village that held out against the invaders!

title: Roman Gaul and the Pont du Gard
text:
After Caesar's conquest, Gaul was part of the huge Roman Empire for about 500 years. The Gauls and Romans gradually mixed: we call this the [Gallo-Roman] civilisation.

The Romans built new towns everywhere, well organised, with straight streets crossing at right angles. In the centre was the forum, a big square for meetings, trade and justice. Lyon, then called Lugdunum, became the capital of Gaul. Paris was called Lutetia.

The towns had magnificent monuments: [amphitheatres] where people watched gladiator fights, like the arenas of Nîmes and Arles, which are still used for shows today; theatres, like the one in Orange; temples, like the Maison Carrée in Nîmes; and [baths], public bathhouses with hot, warm and cold water, where people came to wash, exercise and chat with friends.

To bring fresh water into the towns, the Romans built [aqueducts]. The most famous is the Pont du Gard, built around the year 50 to bring water to Nîmes. It is a giant bridge with three levels of arches, almost 50 metres high, made of enormous stone blocks laid without cement! The whole aqueduct was 50 kilometres long, and the water flowed thanks to a very gentle slope: only 12 metres of drop over its entire length! What precision! The Pont du Gard is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The Romans also built very solid paved roads to connect towns, with milestones showing distances. Some roads in France still follow their route!

The Gauls gradually adopted the language of the Romans, [Latin]. It is from Latin, mixed with a little Gaulish and later Germanic, that the French language was born! They also adopted Roman fashion and Roman gods, and learned to write.

From the 3rd century, Christianity spread in Gaul. In 177, in Lyon, a young Christian slave named Blandina was martyred in the amphitheatre. Later, Saint Martin, a Roman soldier who shared his cloak with a poor man, became bishop of Tours and one of the most popular saints in France.

title: Clovis, king of the Franks
text:
In the 5th century, the Western Roman Empire was collapsing. Peoples from the East, whom the Romans called "barbarians", settled in Gaul: the Visigoths in the south-west, the Burgundians in the east, and the [Franks] in the north. It is from them that France gets its name!

In 481, a 15-year-old became king of a small group of Franks near Tournai (in today's Belgium). His name was Clovis. He was a fearsome and very ambitious warrior.

A famous story shows his character. After a battle, his soldiers had taken a magnificent vase from a church. The bishop asked Clovis to give it back. When the loot was shared out at Soissons, Clovis asked for the vase, but a soldier refused and struck the vase with his axe, saying: "You'll only get what chance gives you!" Clovis said nothing... A year later, while inspecting his troops, he split that soldier's skull with his axe, saying: "Remember the vase of Soissons!"

Clovis married Clotilde, a Christian Burgundian princess. She wanted him to convert. According to legend, during a difficult battle against the Alamanni, Clovis promised to become a Christian if Clotilde's God gave him victory. He won! Around 496 (or a bit later), he was baptised in Reims by Bishop Remigius, along with thousands of his warriors.

This baptism was very important. The Gallo-Roman inhabitants, who were Christians, more easily accepted a king who shared their religion. And the Church supported Clovis.

In 507, Clovis defeated the Visigoths at Vouillé and conquered almost all of Gaul. He chose Paris as his capital. He also had the laws of the Franks written down.

When he died in 511, his kingdom was divided among his four sons, following Frankish custom. His family, the [Merovingians], ruled for almost 300 years.

For centuries, most kings of France were crowned in Reims, in memory of Clovis's baptism. That's why he is sometimes called the first king of France, even though France didn't really exist yet!

title: Charlemagne, emperor of the West
text:
After the Merovingians, a new family took power among the Franks: the Carolingians. Its most famous member was Charles, known as Charlemagne, which means "Charles the Great".

Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768. He was very tall for his time, about 1.90 metres, with a fine moustache. He loved hunting, swimming and hot baths!

He was also a great warrior. During his 46-year reign, he fought a war almost every year. He conquered a huge territory: today's France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria and northern Italy. Some wars, like the one against the Saxons, were very violent.

A famous legend, "The Song of Roland", tells how, in 778, the rearguard of his army was attacked in the Pyrenees at the Roncevaux Pass. Charlemagne's brave nephew, Roland, blew his horn so hard to call for help that he died!

On Christmas Day in the year 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and proclaimed him [emperor]. It was the first time since the fall of Rome that there was an emperor in the West!

To govern his vast empire, Charlemagne divided it into territories ruled by [counts]. He sent inspectors, the missi dominici, who travelled in pairs, a count and a bishop, to check that orders were being followed.

Charlemagne loved learning, even though he found writing hard. He invited the best scholars in Europe to his court at Aachen. He asked monasteries and cathedrals to open schools. A French song even says: "Who had this crazy idea one day to invent school? It was that darned Charlemagne!" (In reality, schools already existed before him, but he developed them a lot.)

Monks copied many ancient books and created a new, clear, easy-to-read handwriting: Carolingian minuscule, the ancestor of our lowercase letters!

Charlemagne died in 814. His empire was then divided among his grandsons...

title: The Oaths of Strasbourg, the first text in French
text:
After Charlemagne's death, his son Louis the Pious became emperor. But when Louis died, his three sons quarrelled over the empire: Lothair, the eldest, wanted to keep everything, while Charles the Bald and Louis the German wanted their share.

Charles and Louis joined forces against their brother Lothair. On the 14th of February 842, in Strasbourg, in front of their armies, they swore a solemn [oath]: they promised to help each other and never to make a separate peace with Lothair.

But there was a problem: their soldiers didn't speak the same language! Louis's soldiers, in the east, spoke a Germanic language, the ancestor of German. Charles's soldiers, in the west, spoke a Romance language born from Latin, the ancestor of French.

So, so that all the soldiers would understand, Louis swore the oath in the language of Charles's soldiers, and Charles swore it in the language of Louis's soldiers! Then each army swore in its own language.

A historian of the time, Nithard, who was the cousin of both kings, wrote down these oaths exactly as they were spoken. And that's where the treasure lies: the Romance text of the Oaths of Strasbourg is the oldest known written text in the French language! Well, in "very old French", which still looks a lot like Latin.

It begins: "Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo et nostro commun salvament..." which means: "For the love of God and for the salvation of the Christian people and our common salvation..." Can you recognise some words?

The following year, in 843, the three brothers made peace with the Treaty of Verdun. Charlemagne's empire was divided into three: in the west, the West Francia of Charles the Bald, which would become France; in the east, the East Francia of Louis, which would become Germany; and in the middle, a long kingdom for Lothair, from the North Sea to Italy.

This division is often seen as the birth certificate of France and Germany.

Over the centuries, this Romance language evolved into [Old French], and then into the French of today, spoken by more than 300 million people around the world!

title: Hugh Capet, the first of the Capetians
text:
In the 9th and 10th centuries, France went through a difficult period. The Carolingian kings had become weak. Invaders attacked the kingdom: the [Vikings], from Scandinavia, sailed up the rivers in their fast longships, raiding towns and monasteries. In 885, they even besieged Paris!

To protect themselves, people turned to local lords, who had soldiers and built castles. This was the beginning of [feudalism]: a powerful lord gave land, a fief, to another lord, his vassal. In exchange, the vassal swore loyalty to him and had to help him in war. The peasants worked the lord's land and received his protection.

In 911, King Charles the Simple even gave a region to the Viking chief Rollo, so that he would protect the kingdom against other Vikings. This region, the land of the "Northmen", became Normandy!

In 987, the last Carolingian king, Louis V, died in a hunting accident without children. The great lords and bishops met in Senlis to choose a new king. They elected Hugh, Duke of the Franks and Count of Paris. He was nicknamed "Capet", perhaps because of the cape he wore as lay abbot of Saint-Martin of Tours.

Hugh Capet was not very powerful. His royal domain was small: an area around Paris and Orléans. Many of his vassals, like the Duke of Normandy or the Count of Flanders, were much richer than he was!

But Hugh Capet was very clever. A few months after his election, he had his son Robert crowned king while he was still alive. That way, when he died, his son was already king, and nobody could elect someone else. His descendants did the same for almost 200 years!

Thanks to this trick, Hugh Capet's family, the Capetians, kept the throne for more than 800 years, until 1848, through the branches of the Valois and the Bourbons. All the kings of France who followed, from Saint Louis to Louis XVI, were his descendants!

Little by little, the Capetian kings enlarged their domain and became more and more powerful.

title: William the Conqueror and the Bayeux Tapestry
text:
Do you remember the Vikings who settled in Normandy? Their descendants, the Normans, became French-speaking Christians and excellent knights. In the 11th century, their leader was Duke William of Normandy.

In January 1066, the King of England, Edward the Confessor, died without children. William said that Edward had promised him the crown. But in London, a powerful English lord, Harold Godwinson, had himself crowned king. William was furious!

He prepared a huge expedition. His men built hundreds of ships and loaded them with soldiers, horses, weapons and even a wooden castle in kit form! In September 1066, the fleet crossed the Channel.

On the 14th of October 1066, the two armies met near Hastings. The English fought on foot behind a wall of shields, on top of a hill. The Norman [knights] charged again and again. At one point, a rumour spread that William was dead! He lifted his helmet so his men could see his face. In the evening, King Harold was killed, perhaps by an arrow in the eye, and the English fled.

On Christmas Day 1066, William was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey. He became "William the Conqueror". For centuries afterwards, the kings of England spoke French, and that is why English has so many French words!

This story is told on an extraordinary work: the Bayeux Tapestry. It is actually an [embroidery], stitched with coloured wool on a long strip of linen. It is almost 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, like a giant comic strip!

It shows more than 600 people, 200 horses, 55 dogs, ships, castles, battles and even Halley's Comet, which crossed the sky in 1066. Short sentences in [Latin] explain the scenes.

It was probably made in England, a few years after the battle, for William's half-brother, Bishop Odo of Bayeux. Almost 1,000 years later, it is still kept in Bayeux, in Normandy.

title: Philip Augustus and the Battle of Bouvines
text:
In 1180, a 15-year-old boy became King of France: Philip II. He would later be nicknamed "Augustus", like the great Roman emperor, because he greatly enlarged the kingdom.

At that time, the King of England was also a French lord. Thanks to marriages and inheritances, the Plantagenet family owned Normandy, Anjou, Aquitaine... more than half of France! They were officially vassals of the King of France, but they were much richer than him.

Philip Augustus decided to take back these lands. Little by little, through war and cunning, he conquered Normandy, Anjou, Maine and Touraine from the English king, John Lackland.

His enemies joined forces against him: John Lackland, the German emperor Otto IV and the Count of Flanders. They wanted to crush the King of France once and for all.

On Sunday the 27th of July 1214, near the village of Bouvines, in the north of France, the two armies met. The king's army was smaller. During the battle, Philip was knocked off his horse and nearly killed by enemy foot soldiers! His [knights] saved him. In the end, the French won a great victory. The emperor fled and the Count of Flanders was taken prisoner.

When the king returned to Paris, people celebrated for a whole week. For the first time, many French people felt proud of their king and their kingdom. Some historians say that this is one of the first moments when a feeling of being "French" appeared.

Philip Augustus also transformed Paris. He surrounded the city with a great wall, paved some streets and built a strong fortress to protect the city: the Louvre! Its old foundations can still be seen today beneath the museum.

He also changed his title: instead of "King of the Franks", he began to call himself "King of France". The king was no longer only the chief of a people, but the ruler of a territory.

title: Saint Louis and the Sainte-Chapelle
text:
Louis IX, the grandson of Philip Augustus, became king in 1226, when he was only 12 years old. His mother, Blanche of Castile, governed for him until he grew up. She was a strong and intelligent queen who taught him to be very religious.

Louis IX wanted to be a just king. Legend says that he sat under an oak tree in the woods of Vincennes, and that anyone, rich or poor, could come and ask him to settle their quarrels. He wanted justice to be the same for everyone.

He forbade private wars between lords and trials by combat, where people fought to decide who was right. He created a single royal currency that could be used everywhere in the kingdom.

He was also very generous to the poor. He founded hospitals, like the Quinze-Vingts in Paris, for 300 blind people. He sometimes served meals to the poor himself.

Louis IX was deeply Christian. He bought from the Emperor of Constantinople a very precious [relic]: the Crown of Thorns, which, according to tradition, had been placed on the head of Jesus. To house it, he had a wonderful chapel built in his palace in Paris: the Sainte-Chapelle, consecrated in 1248.

The Sainte-Chapelle is a jewel of [Gothic] art. Its walls are almost entirely made of [stained glass]: 15 huge windows telling more than 1,000 stories from the Bible! When the sun shines, you feel as if you are inside a treasure chest of light.

In 1248, Louis left for the [Crusades] to the Holy Land. He was taken prisoner in Egypt and had to pay a huge ransom. In 1270, he left on a new crusade and died of illness near Tunis.

After his death, the Church made him a saint. Since then, he has been called "Saint Louis". Many towns, churches and even the city of St. Louis, in the United States, are named after him.

title: The Hundred Years' War and the Black Death
text:
In 1328, the King of France, Charles IV, died without a son. The throne went to his cousin, Philip VI of Valois. But the King of England, Edward III, was the grandson of a French king through his mother. He said: "The crown of France should be mine!"

In 1337, war broke out between the two kingdoms. It lasted, with pauses, until 1453, more than 100 years! That is why it is called the Hundred Years' War.

At first, the English won great victories. At Crécy, in 1346, the English [archers], with their powerful longbows, shot thousands of arrows at the French [knights]. The heavy knights, stuck in the mud, could not do anything. It was a disaster for France.

Then, in 1348, an even more terrible enemy arrived: the [plague]. This disease came from Asia on merchant ships. It was carried by fleas living on rats. People who caught it had a high fever and big black swellings. Most of them died within a few days.

This epidemic was called the "Black Death". In just a few years, it killed about one in three people in Europe! Entire villages were emptied. People did not understand where the disease came from. Some thought it was a punishment from God, others unfairly accused certain groups, like the Jews, who were persecuted.

The war continued, and the countryside suffered terribly. Bands of soldiers without pay, the "Great Companies", robbed and burned villages. Peasants were so desperate that they sometimes revolted.

In 1415, at Agincourt, the French knights were again defeated by the English archers. Then, in 1420, the treaty of Troyes said that the King of England would become King of France! The son of the French king, the [dauphin] Charles, was disinherited. He took refuge south of the Loire.

France seemed lost. But a young girl from Lorraine was going to change everything...

title: Joan of Arc frees Orléans
text:
Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, a small village in Lorraine. She was the daughter of peasants. She could not read or write, but she spun wool and looked after the animals.

When she was 13, she said that she heard voices: those of Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to go and save France and to have the [dauphin] Charles crowned king.

In 1429, when she was 17, she went to see the lord of Vaucouleurs. He first laughed at her, but in the end he gave her an escort. She cut her hair short, dressed as a man and rode for eleven days to reach the dauphin at Chinon.

Legend says that Charles hid among his courtiers to test her, but Joan recognised him immediately! After questioning her for a long time, the dauphin gave her an army.

The city of Orléans had been besieged by the English for months. If it fell, all of France would be lost. Joan arrived with her white banner. She encouraged the soldiers, who regained their courage. In only a few days, in May 1429, the English forts fell, and Orléans was freed! Joan was wounded by an arrow in the shoulder, but she went back to fight. People called her "the Maid of Orléans".

Then she led Charles to Reims, the city where kings were traditionally crowned. On the 17th of July 1429, he became King Charles VII in the cathedral, with Joan standing beside him with her banner.

But in 1430, Joan was captured by the Burgundians, allies of the English, who sold her to the English. She was put on trial by churchmen who supported the English. They accused her of being a [heretic] and a witch. On the 30th of May 1431, she was burned alive in Rouen. She was 19 years old.

The war continued, but in 1453 the English were driven out of France, except from Calais. Twenty-five years after her death, a new trial declared Joan innocent. In 1920, she was made a saint.

title: Francis I, Leonardo da Vinci and the Renaissance
text:
At the end of the Middle Ages, a great movement began in Italy: the [Renaissance], which means "rebirth". Artists and scholars rediscovered the works of ancient Greece and Rome. They painted, sculpted and built with new ideas.

When the young King of France, Francis I, went to war in Italy, he was dazzled by its palaces, paintings and gardens. He wanted to bring the Renaissance to France!

Francis I became king in 1515, when he was 20 years old. That same year, he won the famous battle of Marignano. He was tall, strong, cheerful, and he loved hunting, parties, art and poetry.

He invited the greatest Italian artists to France. The most famous of them was Leonardo da Vinci, painter, engineer and inventor. In 1516, Leonardo crossed the Alps on a mule, carrying some of his paintings, including the Mona Lisa! The king gave him a manor, the Clos Lucé, near the castle of Amboise. Leonardo spent the last three years of his life there. He died in 1519. That is why the Mona Lisa is in the Louvre today!

In 1519, Francis I began to build an extraordinary castle in the middle of a forest full of game: Chambord. It has 426 rooms, 282 fireplaces and a forest of chimneys and turrets on its roof, like a little city in the sky!

At its heart is an amazing double-spiral staircase: two people can climb it at the same time without ever meeting, while still seeing each other through the openings. It may have been inspired by Leonardo's ideas.

Chambord is the most famous of the [châteaux of the Loire], a group of magnificent castles built along the river Loire, such as Chenonceau, Blois or Amboise.

Francis I also loved books. He created a special position for scholars, which later became the Collège de France, and he enriched the royal library. He was a king of the Renaissance!

title: The Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts: French becomes the official language
text:
Today, everyone in France speaks French. But 500 years ago, that was not the case at all!

In the countryside, most people spoke their regional language: Breton in Brittany, [Occitan] in the south, Basque, Alsatian, Flemish, Picard, Provençal... A peasant from Brittany and a peasant from Provence could not understand each other!

And in law courts and official documents, people used [Latin], the language of scholars and the Church. But ordinary people did not understand Latin. When they went to court, they did not always understand the judgement given against them!

In August 1539, in his castle of Villers-Cotterêts, north of Paris, King Francis I signed a big text of 192 articles to reorganise justice: an [ordinance].

Two short articles changed the history of the French language. They said that from then on, all judgements and official documents had to be written "in the French mother tongue, and not otherwise". French thus replaced Latin in the kingdom's official texts!

The same ordinance also asked priests to keep registers of baptisms in each parish. It was the beginning of [civil registration], which allows us to know when and where people were born.

This ordinance is still in force today! It is the oldest French law still applied.

But be careful: people did not all start speaking French overnight. It took centuries. Many children continued to speak their regional language at home until the 20th century. Today, these regional languages are part of the heritage of France, and some are still taught in schools.

In 2023, the castle of Villers-Cotterêts, completely restored, became the International City of the French Language. It is a museum where you can discover the history of French, a language spoken today by more than 300 million people in the world!

title: Henry IV and the Edict of Nantes
text:
In the 16th century, Christians in Europe split into two groups. The [Catholics] remained loyal to the Pope. The [Protestants] followed reformers like Luther and Calvin, who wanted to change the Church. In France, Protestants were also called "Huguenots".

Between the two groups, hatred grew. From 1562, France was torn apart by the Wars of Religion: eight wars in 36 years! Villages were burned, churches destroyed, and people killed because of their faith.

The most terrible day was the 24th of August 1572: the [St Bartholomew's Day massacre]. In Paris, thousands of Protestants were murdered by Catholics. The massacre then spread to other towns.

At that time, a young Protestant prince had just married the king's sister in Paris: Henry of Navarre. He escaped the massacre by agreeing to become Catholic. Later, he returned to Protestantism.

In 1589, King Henry III was killed without children. The heir to the throne was... Henry of Navarre, a Protestant! Many Catholics refused to accept him. He had to fight for years to win his kingdom. In 1593, to bring peace, he became Catholic again. He is said to have declared: "Paris is well worth a Mass!"

In 1598, he signed the Edict of Nantes. This text allowed Protestants to practise their religion in certain places, gave them the same rights as Catholics and granted them fortified towns for their safety. It was one of the first steps towards [religious tolerance] in Europe.

Henry IV then rebuilt the kingdom, ruined by war. With his minister Sully, he developed farming, built roads and canals, and planted mulberry trees for silk. He wanted every peasant family to be able to eat a "chicken in the pot" every Sunday!

He became one of the most popular kings in French history. But in 1610, he was stabbed to death in his carriage in Paris by a fanatic named Ravaillac.

title: Richelieu founds the Académie française
text:
After the death of Henry IV, his son Louis XIII became king. He was only 8 years old! When he grew up, he chose a very clever and very determined minister to help him govern: Cardinal Richelieu.

A [cardinal] is one of the highest leaders of the Catholic Church. Richelieu was a churchman, but above all, he was a statesman. For 18 years, from 1624 to 1642, he worked tirelessly to make the king powerful.

He wanted the king to be obeyed by everyone. He had the fortified castles of rebellious nobles destroyed. He forbade [duels], in which nobles fought with swords, often to the death, over questions of honour. Those who disobeyed were punished severely.

He also fought the Protestants, who had become a kind of state within the state, and besieged their great city of La Rochelle. And he led France into the war against the powerful Habsburgs of Spain and Austria.

You may know Richelieu from "The Three Musketeers" by Alexandre Dumas: in the novel, he is the scheming enemy of d'Artagnan! In reality, he was a great minister, even if he was harsh.

Richelieu also loved literature. He learned that a small group of writers met every week in Paris to talk about the French language. In 1635, he turned this group into an official institution: the Académie française.

Its members, 40 writers and scholars, are nicknamed "the Immortals". Why? Because the motto of the Académie is "To immortality", and because when one of them dies, a new member is elected to replace him. There are always 40!

Their mission is to take care of the French language and to write a [dictionary] that gives the rules and the meaning of words. The first edition was published in 1694. The ninth edition was completed in 2024, almost 90 years after it began!

The Académie française still meets today, under the golden dome of the Institut de France, in Paris.

title: Louis XIV, the Sun King, moves to Versailles
text:
Louis XIV became king in 1643, when he was only 4 years old! When he was a child, he lived through a revolt of nobles and Parisians, the Fronde. He had to flee Paris at night. He never forgot it.

When he began to govern by himself, in 1661, he decided that nobody would ever again threaten the king's power. He governed alone, without a prime minister. He was an [absolute monarch]: he made the laws, led the army and judged, all at the same time.

He chose the Sun as his emblem, because everything revolves around it. That is why he is called "the Sun King".

His father had a small hunting lodge at Versailles, near Paris. Louis XIV transformed it into the most magnificent palace in Europe. Thousands of workers laboured there for years. In 1682, the king and his court moved there for good.

The palace is gigantic: more than 2,000 rooms! The most famous is the Hall of Mirrors, 73 metres long, with 357 mirrors reflecting the light of the gardens. The gardens, designed by André Le Nôtre, have long straight paths, lakes, statues and fountains, and a Grand Canal where the king went boating.

Louis XIV invited the great nobles to live with him at Versailles. His day was organised like a show: getting up, meals, walks, going to bed... Everything followed strict rules called [etiquette]. The nobles competed for the honour of handing him his shirt! In this way, the king kept an eye on them, and they no longer thought of rebelling.

Louis XIV protected the arts: Molière wrote comedies, Lully composed music and Racine wrote tragedies. The king himself loved to dance in ballets!

But he also made many wars, which cost a lot of money and lives. In 1685, he cancelled the Edict of Nantes, and many Protestants had to flee France. He reigned for 72 years, the longest reign in French history, and died in 1715.

title: The Enlightenment and the Encyclopédie
text:
In the 18th century, some thinkers in Europe had a new idea: we should use our [reason] to understand the world, instead of simply believing what we are told. They wanted to bring light into people's minds, to chase away the darkness of ignorance. That is why this period is called the Enlightenment.

In France, these thinkers were called the [philosophers]. The most famous were Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau and Diderot.

Voltaire wrote plays, stories and thousands of letters. He made fun of injustice and fought against intolerance. When a Protestant, Jean Calas, was unfairly executed, Voltaire campaigned for years until his innocence was recognised.

Montesquieu explained that, to avoid tyranny, power must not be held by one person. Those who make the laws, those who apply them and those who judge must be separate. This is the [separation of powers], which is still used in many countries today.

Rousseau wrote that all people are born free and equal, and that laws should express the will of the people.

In 1751, Denis Diderot and the mathematician d'Alembert published the first volume of a gigantic work: the Encyclopédie. Their goal was to gather all human knowledge in one work: science, history, art, but also the crafts of the time, such as how to make paper, glass or bread, with thousands of beautiful illustrations.

More than 150 authors took part. It took more than 20 years and ended up with 28 volumes containing 72,000 articles!

But the Encyclopédie also contained bold ideas. It criticised the privileges of the nobility, intolerance and arbitrary power. The king and the Church banned it several times! Diderot even had to continue working in secret.

These ideas circulated in salons, cafés and books. Little by little, more and more people began to think that the kingdom should change... These ideas prepared the Revolution.

title: The storming of the Bastille
text:
In 1789, France was going through a very difficult time. The kingdom was bankrupt because of wars and the expenses of the court. The harvest of 1788 had been very bad, and the price of bread was soaring. Many people were hungry.

French society was divided into three orders. The clergy (the churchmen) and the nobility had many [privileges]: for example, they paid few taxes. The Third Estate, meaning everybody else, peasants, craftsmen, merchants, 97% of the population, paid almost all the taxes!

To find money, King Louis XVI called the [Estates-General], a big meeting of representatives of the three orders, in Versailles. It opened on the 5th of May 1789. Before that, all over France, people had written down their complaints in notebooks.

But the deputies of the Third Estate felt they were not being listened to. On the 20th of June, locked out of their meeting room, they gathered in a tennis court hall and swore not to separate until they had given France a [constitution]. This was the Tennis Court Oath. They called themselves the National Assembly.

The king gathered soldiers around Paris. The Parisians were afraid that he would dissolve the Assembly by force. They looked for weapons to defend themselves.

On the morning of the 14th of July 1789, a crowd took thousands of rifles at the Invalides. But they needed gunpowder! It was stored at the Bastille, an old fortress-prison, a symbol of the king's arbitrary power.

The crowd surrounded the Bastille. After several hours of fighting, the governor surrendered. The fortress was taken! In fact, there were only seven prisoners inside, but the symbol was huge: the people had defeated the king's power.

The Bastille was demolished stone by stone. The Revolution had begun! Since 1880, the 14th of July has been France's national holiday, celebrated with a military parade and fireworks.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
text:
After the storming of the Bastille, a great fear spread through the countryside. Peasants attacked castles and burned the documents listing what they owed their lords.

To calm things down, on the night of the 4th of August 1789, the deputies of the National Assembly voted for something extraordinary: the abolition of [privileges]! From now on, the nobles and the clergy would no longer have special rights. Everyone would pay taxes according to their means. It was the end of the old [feudal|feudalism] system.

A few weeks later, on the 26th of August 1789, the Assembly adopted a very important text: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its first article says:

"Men are born and remain free and equal in rights."

This sentence was revolutionary! Before, a person's rights depended on their birth: noble or not. Now, the law had to be the same for everyone.

The Declaration contains 17 articles. It says, for example:
- that everyone has the right to freedom, property, safety and resistance to oppression;
- that nobody can be arrested without a reason laid down by law;
- that everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty;
- that everyone has the right to freedom of opinion, including religious opinion, and to express themselves freely;
- that power comes from the nation, that is to say from the people.

It was inspired by the ideas of the Enlightenment philosophers and by the American Declaration of Independence.

But it was not perfect. It forgot women! In 1791, Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, but she was not listened to. And [slavery] continued in the colonies.

Even so, this text changed the world. It inspired the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in Paris in 1948. It is still part of the French [constitution] today.

title: The birth of the Republic
text:
After 1789, France became a [constitutional monarchy]: the king still reigned, but he had to respect a constitution and laws voted by the deputies.

But Louis XVI did not really accept these changes. In June 1791, he tried to flee secretly abroad with his family, disguised as servants! He was recognised and stopped in the town of Varennes, and brought back to Paris. The people lost their trust in him.

In 1792, Austria and Prussia, whose kings were afraid that the Revolution would spread to their countries, went to war against France. Soldiers from Marseille marched to Paris singing a new war song. It was called "La Marseillaise" and later became France's national anthem!

On the 10th of August 1792, the Parisians attacked the Tuileries Palace, where the king lived. Louis XVI was imprisoned with his family.

On the 20th of September 1792, at Valmy, the French army, made up of many volunteers, stopped the Prussians. The soldiers shouted: "Long live the Nation!"

The next day, on the 21st of September 1792, the new assembly, the Convention, abolished the monarchy. France became a [republic], for the first time in its history! The king was no longer in charge: power belonged to the people and their representatives.

Louis XVI, now called "Citizen Louis Capet", was put on trial. He was sentenced to death and executed on the [guillotine] on the 21st of January 1793. His wife, Queen Marie-Antoinette, was executed in October.

Then came a very dark period: the Terror. Leaders such as Robespierre believed the Republic was threatened from all sides. Thousands of people suspected of being its enemies were guillotined. In 1794, Robespierre himself was overthrown and executed.

The symbols of the Republic were born during the Revolution: the blue, white and red flag, La Marseillaise, the motto "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity", and Marianne, a woman wearing a red cap, who represents the Republic.

title: The metre and the metric system
text:
Before the Revolution, measuring things was a real headache! There were hundreds of different units in France: the foot, the inch, the league, the ell, the fathom, the bushel... And they changed from town to town! The Paris foot was not the same length as the Bordeaux foot.

This caused many problems for merchants, who could easily be cheated. The revolutionaries said: "We need the same measurements for everyone!" It was a question of equality.

Scientists decided to create a new unit based on nature, so that it could belong "to all people, for all time". They chose the size of the Earth! The [metre] would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator.

But how could they know this distance? Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, were given a mission: to measure precisely the distance between Dunkirk, in the north of France, and Barcelona, in Spain. Using [triangulation], they measured angles between church towers and hilltops.

The mission lasted seven years, from 1792 to 1799! The astronomers were sometimes arrested as spies, because people did not understand what they were doing with their strange instruments at the top of towers.

In 1795, the metre became the official unit of length. The whole system was based on the number 10, which makes calculations easy. It is the [decimal] system: 1 metre = 10 decimetres = 100 centimetres = 1,000 millimetres.

The gram was created for weight: it is the weight of one cubic centimetre of water. And the litre for volume.

In 1799, a platinum metre bar was made and kept in Paris. There were even marble metres fixed on walls in the streets, so that people could get used to it. Two of them can still be seen in Paris!

Today, almost every country in the world uses the metric system. Only a few, such as the United States, still use other units in daily life.

title: Napoleon Bonaparte, Emperor of the French
From Russia to Waterloo: the fall of Napoleon
text:
In 1812, Napoleon was at the height of his power. But the Tsar of Russia, Alexander I, refused to obey him. Napoleon decided to invade Russia with an enormous army: the Grande Armée, with more than 600,000 soldiers from all over Europe!

The Russians did not want to fight head-on. They retreated, burning everything behind them so the French could find nothing to eat. After a bloody battle at Borodino, Napoleon entered Moscow in September. But the city was deserted, and soon a huge fire destroyed most of it.

The tsar still refused to make peace. Winter was coming. Napoleon had to order the [retreat]. It was a catastrophe! The cold reached -30°C. The soldiers were hungry, exhausted and attacked by Cossack horsemen. Crossing the icy Berezina river cost thousands of lives. Of the Grande Armée, fewer than 100,000 men came back.

All of Europe then rose up against Napoleon. In 1814, the enemy armies entered Paris. Napoleon had to [abdicate], that is to say, give up his throne. He was sent into exile on the small island of Elba, in the Mediterranean. The brother of Louis XVI became king under the name of Louis XVIII.

But in March 1815, Napoleon escaped from Elba! He landed in the south of France with a thousand soldiers. The troops sent to stop him joined him instead, and he entered Paris in triumph. This return lasted about 100 days, and is called the Hundred Days.

On the 18th of June 1815, near the village of Waterloo, in Belgium, Napoleon faced the English army of Wellington and the Prussian army of Blücher. It had rained a lot and the ground was muddy. Late in the day, the Prussians arrived, and the French army was defeated.

Napoleon was sent this time to Saint Helena, a tiny island lost in the Atlantic Ocean. He died there in 1821. In 1840, his body was brought back to Paris, to the Invalides, where his tomb can still be seen today.

title: Niépce and Daguerre invent photography
text:
For a long time, the only way to keep an image of a person or a landscape was to draw or paint it. And that took a lot of time and talent!

Since ancient times, people had known about the [camera obscura]: a dark box with a small hole. Light entering through the hole projects an upside-down image of the outside on the opposite wall. Artists used it to draw. But how could this image be captured for good?

Nicéphore Niépce, an inventor from Burgundy, worked on this problem for years. He coated a plate with a kind of asphalt that hardens in the light. Around 1826 or 1827, from the window of his house in Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, he put his plate in a camera obscura and waited... for many hours, perhaps even several days!

The result: a blurry image of the rooftops and courtyard seen from his window. It is the oldest photograph that still exists in the world! It is called "View from the Window at Le Gras".

Niépce then worked with Louis Daguerre, a painter who created huge theatre sets. After Niépce's death in 1833, Daguerre continued the research. He discovered a better method, using a silver-plated copper plate and mercury vapour. The pose time went down to a few minutes.

In 1839, the French state bought the invention and offered it to the whole world for free. It was called the [daguerreotype]. It was a huge success! Everyone wanted their portrait. But you had to stay perfectly still for a long time, sometimes with your head held by a support.

At the same time, in England, William Henry Fox Talbot invented another method that allowed several copies of a photo to be printed.

Photography changed the world. For the first time, people could see real images of faraway places, of wars, of famous people. And today, with our phones, we take billions of photos every day!

title: 1848: the abolition of slavery and universal suffrage
text:
For more than two centuries, France practised [slavery] in its colonies in the Caribbean, in the Indian Ocean and in French Guiana. Men, women and children were captured in Africa and taken across the Atlantic Ocean in slave ships, in terrible conditions. This was the [slave trade].

In the colonies, the enslaved people were considered property, not people. They were forced to work very hard on sugar cane plantations, without pay, and were often beaten. Many rebelled or fled.

The Revolution abolished slavery in 1794, after a great revolt in Saint-Domingue (today Haiti). But Napoleon brought it back in 1802. Haiti, led by former slaves, became independent in 1804.

In February 1848, a new revolution broke out in Paris. King Louis-Philippe was overthrown, and the Second Republic was proclaimed.

A man had been fighting for years against slavery: Victor Schœlcher. He had travelled to the colonies and seen the suffering of the enslaved people. The new government made him responsible for this question. He said: "The Republic cannot allow slavery."

On the 27th of April 1848, the government signed the decree for the abolition of slavery. About 250,000 people were freed in the French colonies! Unfairly, the former slave owners received compensation, but the freed people received nothing.

In the same year, 1848, another great change took place: [universal suffrage]. From then on, all men aged 21 and over could vote, rich or poor! Before, only the richest could vote. The number of voters went from 250,000 to 9 million!

But be careful: it was not really "universal", because women were still not allowed to vote. They had to wait until 1944.

Today, in France, the 10th of May is a day to remember the slave trade, slavery and their abolition. In 2001, a law recognised them as a crime against humanity.

title: The French colonial empire
Baron Haussmann transforms Paris
text:
In 1848, Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon I, was elected president of the Republic. In 1851, he took power by force, and the following year he became emperor under the name of Napoleon III. It was the Second Empire.

At that time, Paris was an overcrowded, dirty and dangerous city. The streets were narrow, dark and winding. There was not enough water, and sewage flowed in the gutters. Diseases like [cholera] killed thousands of people.

Napoleon III wanted to make Paris a modern, healthy and beautiful capital. In 1853, he entrusted this huge task to the [prefect] of the Seine: Baron Georges-Eugène Haussmann.

For 17 years, Paris was one big building site! Thousands of old houses were demolished. In their place, wide straight avenues and boulevards were built, lined with trees, like the Boulevard Saint-Germain or the Avenue de l'Opéra.

Along them, Haussmann had elegant stone buildings constructed, all of the same height and style, with balconies on the second and fifth floors. These "Haussmann-style buildings" still give Paris its look today.

Under the streets, the engineer Belgrand built 600 kilometres of [sewers] and brought clean water from sources far away. Street lights, benches, public toilets and newspaper kiosks appeared. Big parks were created, like the Bois de Boulogne and the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, as well as small squares in each district.

New train stations and a big market, Les Halles, were built. And the famous Opéra Garnier!

But these works also had a downside. The poorest families were driven out of the centre because the rents became too expensive. And some people said the wide avenues were also made so that the army could move easily and stop revolts.

Today, millions of tourists admire Haussmann's Paris.

title: Jules Ferry: free, secular and compulsory school
text:
In 1870, Napoleon III was defeated by Prussia and taken prisoner. The Third Republic was proclaimed. It lasted 70 years!

The leaders of the new Republic thought that, for democracy to work, all citizens had to be educated. How can you vote well if you cannot read a newspaper? But at that time, many children did not go to school. They worked in the fields or in factories from a very young age. Many adults could not read.

Jules Ferry, Minister of Public Instruction, passed two great laws.

In 1881, primary school became free: parents no longer had to pay.

In 1882, school became compulsory for all children, girls and boys, from 6 to 13 years old. And public school became [secular]: religion was no longer taught there. Pupils had a day off, Thursday, so that families who wished could send their children to religious classes.

Thousands of schools were built all over France, often with the town hall in the same building. Each one had a boys' side and a girls' side. Teachers were trained in special schools. They were nicknamed the "black hussars of the Republic", because of their black clothes and their mission.

In the classroom, children wrote with a dip pen and ink, sat at wooden desks and learned to read, write, count, as well as history, geography, science and "moral and civic instruction". There was a map of France on the wall. Every day began with a moral lesson written on the blackboard.

At the end of primary school, pupils could take an exam: the [certificat d'études]. Getting it was a great source of pride for the whole family!

Thanks to these laws, by 1900 almost all young French people could read and write. The school also spread the French language throughout the country, sometimes by forbidding children to speak their regional language.

Unfortunately, Jules Ferry was also a strong supporter of colonisation...

title: Louis Pasteur and the rabies vaccine
text:
Louis Pasteur was born in 1822 in the Jura, the son of a tanner. At school, he was not a brilliant pupil, but he was very patient and loved to draw. He became a chemist and a great scientist.

At the time, nobody understood why milk went sour, why wine became vinegar, or why wounds became infected. Pasteur discovered that it was because of tiny living things, invisible to the naked eye: [microbes]!

He showed that microbes do not appear by themselves: they come from the air, from dust, from dirty hands. He invented a way to kill them by heating food: [pasteurisation]. Today, the milk you drink is still pasteurised!

He also understood that many diseases are caused by microbes. Thanks to him, doctors began to wash their hands, to boil their instruments and to disinfect wounds. This saved millions of lives.

Then Pasteur studied [vaccines]. The idea: give the body a weakened microbe, so that it learns to defend itself without getting sick. He first made vaccines for animals, against chicken cholera and anthrax, a disease that killed sheep.

Then he worked on a terrible disease: rabies. It is transmitted by the bite of a sick animal, often a dog. Once the disease starts, it is almost always deadly.

On the 6th of July 1885, a mother arrived in Paris with her son, Joseph Meister, 9 years old. He had been bitten 14 times by a rabid dog! Pasteur hesitated: his vaccine had only been tested on animals. He was not a doctor, but doctors helped him. For ten days, Joseph received injections. And... he did not get rabies! He was saved!

This news went around the world. People donated money to build the Pasteur Institute in Paris, which opened in 1888. It still exists and fights diseases all over the world.

Joseph Meister later became the caretaker of the Pasteur Institute, where he worked for the rest of his life.

title: The Eiffel Tower and the World's Fair
text:
In 1889, France celebrated the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. To mark the occasion, a huge [World's Fair] was organised in Paris. Countries from all over the world came to present their inventions, their products and their cultures.

For this fair, the organisers wanted a spectacular monument that would show the skill of French engineers. The company of the engineer Gustave Eiffel, who had already built bridges and the internal structure of the Statue of Liberty, proposed an incredible project: an iron tower 300 metres high! It would be the tallest building in the world.

Construction began in January 1887. The tower was made of 18,000 iron parts, assembled with 2.5 million [rivets]! The parts were prepared in the factory with great precision, then assembled on site by about 250 workers, like a giant construction kit. Despite the height, there was only one fatal accident during the work.

In only two years and two months, the tower was finished, just in time for the opening of the fair, in May 1889.

But many people hated it! Famous artists and writers signed a petition against this "useless and monstrous tower" that would disfigure Paris. Some called it a "giant factory chimney".

The tower was supposed to be demolished after 20 years. But Gustave Eiffel had a good idea: he used it for scientific experiments, especially for [radio]. The antennas at the top turned out to be very useful to the army. The tower was saved!

Today, the Eiffel Tower is the symbol of Paris and of France. It is 330 metres high with its antennas. It is repainted every seven years by hand: it takes about 60 tonnes of paint! Every evening, it sparkles with 20,000 light bulbs for five minutes every hour.

More than 6 million people visit it each year. You can climb 674 steps to the second floor... or take the lift!

title: The Lumière brothers invent cinema
text:
Auguste and Louis Lumière were two brothers from Lyon. Their father owned a factory that made [photographic plates]. The brothers were talented inventors. And their name "Lumière" means "light": perfect for inventors of images!

At the end of the 19th century, many inventors were trying to make images move. In America, Thomas Edison had invented the kinetoscope, but only one person at a time could watch the film, by looking into a box.

The Lumière brothers had a better idea. In 1895, they invented the [cinématographe]: a single machine that could film, develop and project moving images onto a large screen, so that many people could watch together! Inside, a clever mechanism, inspired by the sewing machine, moved the film forward, image by image, 16 times per second.

Their first film showed workers leaving their factory in Lyon. It lasted less than a minute!

On the 28th of December 1895, in a room in a café in Paris, the Grand Café, the Lumière brothers organised the first paid public cinema screening in history. Thirty-three spectators paid one franc each to watch ten short films. It was a sensation!

One of the most famous films shows a train arriving at the station of La Ciotat. Legend says that some spectators were so frightened that they jumped out of their seats, fearing the train would come out of the screen!

The Lumière brothers also made the first comedy film: "The Waterer Watered", in which a boy plays a trick on a gardener with his hose.

They sent camera operators all over the world to film cities and people. They made more than 1,400 short films!

Another Frenchman, Georges Méliès, a magician, understood that cinema could also tell imaginary stories. In 1902, he made "A Trip to the Moon", with special effects. Cinema had become an art: the "seventh art"!

title: Marie Curie, winner of two Nobel Prizes
text:
Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 in Warsaw, in Poland, which was then ruled by Russia. She was a brilliant pupil, but at that time, women were not allowed to study at university in her country.

So she worked as a governess to pay for her sister's studies in Paris. Then, in 1891, it was her turn: she went to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne. She was so poor that she sometimes fainted from hunger! But she finished top of her class.

In Paris, she met a physicist, Pierre Curie. They fell in love and married in 1895. She became Marie Curie.

In 1896, the scientist Henri Becquerel discovered that a metal, uranium, gives off mysterious rays. Marie decided to study this phenomenon. She called it [radioactivity].

With Pierre, in a poorly heated shed, she worked for years on tonnes of a mineral called pitchblende. They crushed it, heated it and dissolved it, stirring huge cauldrons with iron bars. In 1898, they discovered two new [chemical elements]: polonium, named after Poland, and radium, which glows in the dark!

In 1903, Marie and Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel received the [Nobel Prize] in Physics. Marie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize!

In 1906, Pierre died, run over by a horse-drawn carriage. Marie was devastated, but she continued. She became the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne. In 1911, she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences!

During the First World War, she created radiology cars, the "little Curies", to X-ray wounded soldiers near the front, and drove them herself.

But nobody knew yet that radioactivity is dangerous. Marie Curie died in 1934 of an illness caused by the radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive today! In 1995, she entered the Panthéon.

title: The law of 1905: separation of Churches and State
text:
For centuries, the kings of France had been crowned in a cathedral, and the Catholic Church had great power in the kingdom. After the Revolution, the state still paid the priests, pastors and rabbis, and religion played an important role in public life.

At the end of the 19th century, there were strong quarrels between two camps. Some wanted the Catholic Church to keep its influence. Others, the republicans, thought that religion should be a private matter and that the Republic should be neutral.

In 1905, after much debate, the deputies passed an important law, prepared by Aristide Briand: the law on the separation of the Churches and the State.

It says two main things:
- the Republic guarantees [freedom of conscience]: everyone is free to believe in a religion or not, and to practise their religion freely, as long as they respect public order;
- the Republic does not recognise or pay for any religion: the state and the religions are separate.

This is the principle of [laïcité], or secularism.

At first, the law caused tension. Some Catholics were angry, especially when officials came to make inventories of the goods in the churches. But over time, calm returned.

Churches built before 1905, like the cathedrals, belong to the state or the towns, which maintain them, but they are made available to believers for free for their services.

Laïcité protects everyone. The state does not favour any religion, and all citizens are equal, whether they are Catholic, Protestant, Jewish, Muslim, Buddhist, of another religion or not religious at all.

In public schools, teachers must be neutral, and since 2004, pupils may not wear conspicuous religious symbols.

Every year, on the 9th of December, schools in France celebrate "Laïcité Day", in memory of the law of 1905.

title: The Great War and the Battle of Verdun
text:
In the summer of 1914, the great powers of Europe were divided into two camps. France, the United Kingdom and Russia on one side; Germany and Austria-Hungary on the other. On the 28th of June, the heir to the Austrian throne was killed in Sarajevo. In a few weeks, all of Europe was at war!

In August 1914, millions of young French men were [mobilised]. Many thought the war would be short and that they would be home for Christmas. It lasted more than four years!

After the first battles, the armies dug [trenches]: long ditches stretching 700 kilometres, from the North Sea to Switzerland. The soldiers, nicknamed the "poilus" (the hairy ones), lived there in mud, cold and rats, under shells. Between the enemy trenches was "no man's land", full of barbed wire and craters.

New and terrible weapons appeared: machine guns, heavy artillery, poison gas, tanks and aeroplanes.

In February 1916, the German army attacked Verdun, a fortified city in the east of France. The battle lasted 300 days! Millions of shells fell on a small area. Forests and villages disappeared. More than 300,000 French and German soldiers were killed, and many more wounded. Most French soldiers fought there at some point, thanks to a rotation system. A single road, the "Sacred Way", brought supplies and fresh troops, with a truck passing every few seconds.

The French held firm, shouting: "They shall not pass!"

In 1917, the United States entered the war alongside France. Soldiers from the colonies also fought for France.

On the 11th of November 1918, at 11 o'clock, the [armistice] was signed. The fighting stopped! Bells rang throughout France.

The war killed about 1.4 million French soldiers. In almost every town and village in France, you can see a [war memorial] with the names of the dead. Every 11th of November, France remembers them.

title: The Popular Front and the first paid holidays
text:
In the 1930s, times were hard. A great economic crisis, which began in 1929 in the United States, reached France. Many factories closed and many workers lost their jobs. At the same time, in Italy and Germany, dictators had taken power: Mussolini and Hitler.

In France, left-wing parties, the socialists, the communists and the radicals, decided to join forces against the crisis and the danger of [fascism]. This alliance was called the Popular Front.

In May 1936, the Popular Front won the elections. Its leader, Léon Blum, became head of the government. He was the first socialist and the first Jewish person to hold this position.

Even before he took office, a huge wave of [strikes] swept through France. Two million workers stopped working and occupied their factories. But it was a joyful strike: people danced, played music and played cards in the workshops!

In June 1936, the government, the employers and the [trade unions] signed the Matignon Agreements. And laws changed the lives of workers:
- wages were increased;
- the working week went down to 40 hours;
- and, for the first time, every worker was entitled to two weeks of [paid holidays] per year!

It was a revolution in everyday life. For the first time, many workers could go on holiday, and still be paid! A minister, Léo Lagrange, organised cheaper train tickets. In the summer of 1936, hundreds of thousands of families discovered the sea, the mountains or the countryside, often by bike or tandem, sleeping in tents or in youth hostels. Many children saw the sea for the first time!

The Popular Front did not last long: Léon Blum's government fell in 1937. But paid holidays remained. Today, workers in France have five weeks of paid holidays per year.

title: Defeat, the Occupation and the Appeal of 18 June
text:
In September 1939, Hitler's Germany invaded Poland. France and the United Kingdom declared war on Germany: the Second World War had begun.

In May 1940, the German army attacked. With its tanks and planes, it advanced very quickly. The French army was defeated in six weeks! Millions of French people fled south on the roads, on foot, by bike or in carts: this was the exodus.

Marshal Pétain, an old hero of Verdun, became head of the government. On the 17th of June, he announced on the radio that the fighting must stop. He signed an [armistice] with Hitler.

But a French general refused defeat: Charles de Gaulle. He left for London. On the 18th of June 1940, on the BBC radio, he called on the French to continue the fight: "Whatever happens, the flame of French resistance must not and will not go out." Few people heard this appeal, but it became famous. It was the birth of Free France.

France was cut in two. The north and the west were occupied by the German army. In the south, Pétain set up a government in Vichy, which ended the Republic. He chose to [collaborate] with the Nazis.

The Vichy regime passed laws against the Jews. They were excluded from many jobs, and from 1942 they had to wear a yellow star in the occupied zone. In July 1942, in Paris, more than 13,000 Jewish men, women and children were arrested by the French police: the Vél' d'Hiv Roundup. About 75,000 Jews were deported from France to the Nazi camps, where most were murdered. It was the [Holocaust].

Some people helped Jews to hide, especially children. They are honoured as the "Righteous Among the Nations".

Men and women also entered the [Resistance]. They printed secret newspapers, sabotaged railways and gathered intelligence for the Allies. Jean Moulin united the movements. Many were arrested, tortured or shot.

title: D-Day, the Liberation and women's right to vote
text:
By 1944, Germany was losing the war. The Soviet army was advancing from the east, and the Allies, the Americans, the British, the Canadians and others, were preparing a huge operation to free Western Europe.

On the 6th of June 1944, D-Day, the largest seaborne invasion in history took place on the beaches of Normandy. That night, thousands of [paratroopers] had jumped behind the German lines. At dawn, about 7,000 ships and 150,000 soldiers arrived off the coast. On beaches with code names like Omaha, Utah, Gold, Juno and Sword, the soldiers had to cross the sand under enemy fire. Among them were 177 French commandos.

The fighting in Normandy lasted all summer and was very hard. Many soldiers and civilians were killed, and towns like Caen and Saint-Lô were almost completely destroyed.

On the 15th of August 1944, another landing took place in Provence, with a large French army, including many soldiers from Africa.

In Paris, the [Resistance] launched an uprising on the 19th of August. Barricades went up in the streets. On the 25th of August, the French 2nd Armoured Division of General Leclerc entered the city, followed by the Americans. The German general surrendered. Paris was free!

The next day, General de Gaulle walked down the Champs-Élysées, cheered by an enormous crowd. France was gradually liberated. The war in Europe ended on the 8th of May 1945, with Germany's surrender.

A new era began. On the 21st of April 1944, a decision had given French women the [right to vote], at last! On the 29th of April 1945, they voted for the first time, in local elections. Women had played a great role in the Resistance and the war, and the Republic finally recognised them as full citizens.

After the war, France was rebuilt. The [social security] system was created in 1945, so that everyone could be cared for when ill, and receive a pension in old age.

title: The Fifth Republic and the end of the Algerian War
text:
After the Second World War, France had a new republic, the Fourth Republic. But governments changed very often: 22 governments in 12 years! It was difficult to make big decisions.

At the same time, the colonised peoples demanded their [independence]. After a long war, France left Indochina in 1954. That same year, the Algerian War began.

Algeria had been French for more than 120 years. About one million Europeans lived there, often born there. But the nine million Algerian Muslims did not have the same rights. The Algerian nationalists of the FLN started an armed struggle for independence.

The war was very cruel on both sides: attacks, massacres, torture. Young French soldiers were sent to fight there. In France, people were deeply divided.

In 1958, the crisis became so serious that people feared a civil war. General de Gaulle, the hero of the Liberation, was called back to power.

He had a new [constitution] written. It gave more power to the President of the Republic. It was adopted by a [referendum] on the 28th of September 1958, with almost 80% "yes". This was the birth of the Fifth Republic, which still exists today! De Gaulle became its first president.

Since 1962, the president has been elected directly by all citizens.

De Gaulle understood that Algeria wanted its independence. After difficult negotiations, the Évian Agreements were signed in March 1962. On the 5th of July 1962, Algeria became independent.

Almost a million Europeans of Algeria, the "pieds-noirs", had to leave for France, often in great distress. The harkis, Algerians who had fought alongside the French army, were abandoned, and many were killed. The war caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.

In the same years, most French colonies in Africa, such as Senegal, Madagascar and Côte d'Ivoire, also became independent countries, mostly peacefully, in 1960.

title: May 68
text:
In 1968, France was prosperous. Since the war, the economy had grown very fast: people bought cars, fridges and televisions. It was the period of the "Thirty Glorious Years".

But many young people felt stifled. Society was very strict. At university, girls and boys lived in separate buildings. At home, at school and at work, you had to obey without discussion. Young people wanted more [freedom], and many dreamed of a fairer world.

It started with the students. In March 1968, at the University of Nanterre, near Paris, students protested. In May, the protest spread to the Sorbonne, in Paris. The police intervened.

On the night of the 10th of May, students built [barricades] in the streets of the Latin Quarter, with paving stones and cars. The police charged. There were hundreds of injured people. Many French people were shocked by the violence.

Then the workers joined in. On the 13th of May, a huge demonstration took place. Then the country went on [strike]: about 7 to 9 million workers stopped working! Factories, trains, post offices, shops... everything stopped. There was no more petrol at the pumps!

On the walls, people wrote poetic slogans: "Imagination to power!", "It is forbidden to forbid!", "Under the paving stones, the beach!"

At the end of May, the government, the employers and the unions signed the Grenelle agreements: the minimum wage was increased by 35%! On the 30th of May, a large demonstration in support of General de Gaulle took place. He dissolved the National Assembly, and new elections were won by his supporters. Little by little, work started again.

May 68 did not overthrow the government, but it changed society. Relations between parents and children, teachers and pupils, men and women became more relaxed. The fight for women's rights grew stronger. In 1974, the voting age was lowered from 21 to 18.

title: Concorde, the TGV and Ariane: France of technology
text:
In the 1960s and 1970s, France wanted to show the world that it was a great modern nation. It launched huge technological projects, often with its European neighbours.

The most famous is Concorde! This passenger plane was built by France and the United Kingdom. On the 2nd of March 1969, it made its first flight from Toulouse. With its slender shape and its "beak" that tilted down for landing, it looked like a white bird.

Concorde was [supersonic]: it flew at more than twice the speed of sound, about 2,200 km/h! It crossed the Atlantic, from Paris to New York, in about 3.5 hours, instead of 8. Passengers could arrive in New York before the time they had left Paris, thanks to the time difference!

But Concorde was very noisy and very expensive. Only 20 were built. After a terrible accident in 2000, it stopped flying in 2003. Today, you can see it in museums.

On the ground, France developed a very fast train: the TGV, "train à grande vitesse" (high-speed train). The first line, between Paris and Lyon, opened in 1981. The journey went from almost 4 hours to 2 hours! In 2007, a specially prepared TGV set the world speed record for a train on rails: 574.8 km/h!

Today, TGV lines connect most of France's big cities.

In space, too, France was ambitious. It created a space centre in Kourou, in French Guiana, close to the Equator, the best place to launch rockets. With its European partners, it built the Ariane [rocket]. The first launch took place on the 24th of December 1979. Ariane rockets have since put hundreds of satellites into [orbit], for television, weather forecasts and telephones.

In 1982, Jean-Loup Chrétien became the first French [astronaut] to go into space, and in 2016, Thomas Pesquet flew to the International Space Station.

title: The abolition of the death penalty
text:
