For a very long time, in France, people who had committed the most serious crimes could be sentenced to death. Since the Revolution, they were executed by the [guillotine], a machine with a heavy blade that cut off the head.

Executions were public until 1939. Then they took place in secret, in the courtyard of prisons. The last execution in France took place in 1977.

Robert Badinter was a lawyer. His father, a Jew, had been deported and killed by the Nazis during the war. Badinter was deeply opposed to the death penalty. In 1972, he defended a man who had not killed anyone, but who had been an accomplice of a murderer. His client was sentenced to death and guillotined. Badinter never recovered from this. From then on, he fought against the death penalty with all his strength.

He believed that:
- a society must not kill, even to punish;
- justice can make mistakes, and an innocent person could be executed, with no possibility of repairing the error;
- the death penalty does not prevent crimes.

In 1981, François Mitterrand was elected President of the Republic. He had promised to abolish the death penalty, even though most French people were in favour of it at the time, according to surveys. He appointed Robert Badinter Minister of Justice.

On the 17th of September 1981, Badinter gave a famous speech to the deputies. He said: "Tomorrow, thanks to you, French justice will no longer be a justice that kills."

The law was passed. On the 9th of October 1981, France [abolished|abolish] the death penalty. Since 2007, it has been written into the [constitution].

Robert Badinter continued to fight all his life for human rights and for the abolition of the death penalty everywhere in the world. He died in February 2024. In October 2025, he entered the Panthéon, where France honours its great people.

title: Building Europe and the euro
text:
France and Germany fought three terrible wars against each other between 1870 and 1945. After the Second World War, some people had a brave idea: to unite the countries of Europe so that war between them would become impossible.

On the 9th of May 1950, the French minister Robert Schuman proposed that France and Germany put their coal and steel together, the materials needed to make weapons. In 1957, six countries, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, signed the Treaty of Rome. They created the European Economic Community.

In 1963, General de Gaulle and the German chancellor Adenauer signed a friendship treaty. The former enemies became friends! Today, young French and German people often take part in exchanges.

Little by little, more countries joined. In 1992, the [Maastricht Treaty] created the European Union. Its citizens can live, study and work freely in all the countries of the Union. The [Schengen Area] allows people to cross most borders without showing a passport.

The Maastricht Treaty also planned a common currency. On the 1st of January 2002, euro coins and banknotes arrived in people's pockets! In France, the euro replaced the franc, which had been used for centuries. One euro was worth about 6.56 francs. At first, people converted all prices in their heads!

Euro coins have a common side and a national side. On French coins, you can find Marianne, a tree or a sower. The banknotes show bridges, windows and gates, symbols of openness and connection between Europeans.

Today, the European Union has 27 member countries and about 450 million inhabitants. The euro is used by 21 countries: Bulgaria adopted it in 2026.

The European Union has its own [parliament], elected by the citizens every five years. Part of its work is in Strasbourg, in France. The EU has a flag with twelve golden stars on a blue background, and an anthem: Beethoven's "Ode to Joy".

title: France becomes football world champion
text:
Football is the most popular sport in France. But for a long time, the French team had never won the most important competition: the [World Cup].

Yet it was a Frenchman, Jules Rimet, who created the World Cup, in 1930! The first trophy even bore his name.

In 1998, France organised the World Cup for the second time, 60 years after the first time. Thirty-two teams from all over the world came to play in ten French cities. A brand-new stadium was built for the occasion: the Stade de France, in Saint-Denis, near Paris.

The French team, "les Bleus", was coached by Aimé Jacquet. There were great players: Zinedine Zidane, the goalkeeper Fabien Barthez, the captain Didier Deschamps, Lilian Thuram, Thierry Henry, Marcel Desailly...

Match after match, the Bleus progressed. In the semi-final against Croatia, the defender Lilian Thuram, who almost never scored, scored twice! France was in the final for the first time in its history.

On the 12th of July 1998, at the Stade de France, France played Brazil, the reigning world champion, with the great Ronaldo. And... France won 3-0! Zidane scored two goals with his head, and Emmanuel Petit scored the third at the very end.

That night, more than a million people poured onto the Champs-Élysées in Paris to celebrate. All over France, people sang, honked their horns and waved flags. Zidane's face was projected onto the Arc de Triomphe.

The French team had players whose families came from many places: Guadeloupe, Algeria, Armenia, Ghana, New Caledonia, Senegal... People spoke of a team "black, blanc, beur" (black, white and Arab) that reflected the [diversity] of France.

France has since won the World Cup a second time, in 2018 in Russia, with Didier Deschamps as coach! And the women's team, "les Bleues", is also one of the best in the world.

title: The fire and rebirth of Notre-Dame de Paris
text:
Notre-Dame de Paris is one of the most famous cathedrals in the world. Its construction began in 1163, in the Middle Ages, and lasted almost 200 years. It is a masterpiece of [Gothic] art, with its two towers, its gargoyles, its flying buttresses and its large [rose windows].

It has witnessed the whole history of France: Napoleon was crowned there, and bells rang there for the Liberation of Paris. The writer Victor Hugo made it famous with his novel "The Hunchback of Notre-Dame", in 1831.

On the evening of the 15th of April 2019, a fire broke out in the roof, during restoration work. In a few hours, the flames destroyed the roof frame, made of ancient oak beams and nicknamed "the forest". Around the world, millions of people watched on television, in shock. At 7:50 p.m., the spire, 96 metres high, collapsed!

About 600 firefighters fought all night. They managed to save the two towers, the bells, the rose windows and the treasures of the cathedral, including the Crown of Thorns, bought by Saint Louis. Inside, a human chain carried the precious objects to safety.

The President of the Republic, Emmanuel Macron, promised to rebuild the cathedral in five years. Donations came from all over the world.

It was a gigantic building site. Hundreds of [craftspeople] worked there: stonemasons, carpenters, roofers, glassmakers, organ builders... The frame was rebuilt as in the Middle Ages, with about 2,000 oak trees from French forests, cut with axes. The spire was rebuilt identically, with a golden rooster at the top.

The stones were cleaned: the cathedral has never been so bright! The great organ, with its 8,000 pipes, was also dismantled, cleaned and reassembled.

On the 7th and 8th of December 2024, after five years of work, Notre-Dame de Paris reopened its doors. Its bells rang out again over Paris. Millions of visitors have come back to admire it.

title: The Paris 2024 Olympic Games
text:
The modern [Olympic Games] were created by a Frenchman: Baron Pierre de Coubertin. He wanted to revive the Games of ancient Greece to bring together young people from all over the world through sport. The first modern Games took place in Athens in 1896.

Paris had already hosted the Games in 1900 and 1924. One hundred years later, in 2024, it was Paris's turn again!

The opening ceremony, on the 26th of July 2024, was like no other. For the first time, it did not take place in a stadium, but along the Seine! About 85 boats carried the athletes along the river, over 6 kilometres, in front of the monuments of Paris. There were dancers, singers, horse riders and surprises everywhere, despite the rain.

At the end, the Olympic [cauldron] was lit in the Tuileries Garden: a large ring of fire rising into the sky under a hot-air balloon, a tribute to the first hot-air balloon flight, in Paris, in 1783!

The competitions took place in magnificent places: beach volleyball at the foot of the Eiffel Tower, fencing under the glass roof of the Grand Palais, horse riding in the gardens of Versailles, and surfing... in Tahiti, in French Polynesia!

About 10,500 athletes from 206 teams took part. For the first time, there were exactly as many women as men.

France won 64 medals, including 16 gold medals! The swimmer Léon Marchand became the star of the Games, winning four gold medals. The judoka Teddy Riner won his fifth Olympic gold medal, a record!

A few days later, the [Paralympic Games] took place, for athletes with disabilities. The French public cheered them on with just as much enthusiasm.

During the summer, millions of spectators and volunteers made Paris a huge celebration. Even the Seine had been cleaned up, and swimming there will be possible again, a hundred years after it was banned!

title: France today
text:
Here we are in France today! What is it like?

France has about 69 million inhabitants. It is a democratic [republic]. Its motto is "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity". Its symbols are the blue, white and red flag, La Marseillaise, Marianne, the rooster and the national holiday on the 14th of July. Its president is elected for five years by all citizens over 18.

Mainland France, nicknamed "the Hexagon" because of its six-sided shape, has very varied landscapes: mountains like the Alps, with Mont Blanc, the highest peak in Western Europe (4,805 metres), the Pyrenees and the Massif Central; coasts on the English Channel, the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea; and great rivers like the Loire, the Seine, the Rhône and the Garonne. But France also includes [overseas territories], in the Caribbean, South America, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. Thanks to them, the sun never sets on France!

France is the most visited country in the world: about 100 million foreign tourists come each year to admire its monuments, museums and landscapes, and to taste its food. The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world!

French cuisine is famous all over the world: bread and the baguette (added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage in 2022!), croissants, more than 1,000 kinds of cheese, crêpes, ratatouille, bouillabaisse... The French gastronomic meal is also on the UNESCO list.

French is spoken by more than 320 million people on five continents. The countries that share this language form the [Francophonie]. More than half of French speakers live in Africa! And in France, people also speak regional languages such as Breton, Basque, Occitan, Alsatian, Corsican and Creole.

France is a diverse society: many French people have parents or grandparents who came from other countries, from Europe, Africa, Asia or elsewhere. This diversity is part of its richness.

France faces great challenges: [climate change], which causes heatwaves, droughts and floods; protecting nature; and the need for very different people to live together in peace and justice.

The history of France continues to be written, from Tautavel Man all the way to you. And you, what would you like to add to it?
